_readme: The citation register: the only place the agent's acts, regulations, sections and cases are listed. It is added to the prompt by api/chat.ts, grouped by instrument `group` (field, q1, q2, q3), with each instrument's `use` note (when and how to apply it). Each check has an id; the agent cites a provision by its id, and the other prompt files refer to provisions by id too (`npm run citations:lint` fails the build if one of them names an id that does not exist or writes out a citation that belongs here). Each check records what the agent is told (claim), what the official source actually says (sourceSays), and the result: correct, partly_correct, wrong, invented or unchecked. Only set a result other than unchecked after reading the provision on Ontario e-Laws (ontario.ca/laws), the federal Justice Laws Website (laws-lois.justice.gc.ca), the Supreme Court of Canada site, PEO or Engineers Canada, or, for a by-law, the municipality's official consolidation (for Toronto, toronto.ca/legdocs/municode), and fill in checked (YYYY-MM-DD). `uncertain: true` tells the agent the section number has not been confirmed. An optional note is a reminder for whoever checks the entry; it is not sent to the agent. Never change an existing id: past assessments refer to it. Run `npm run citations:table` to print the register as a Markdown table for the report.

tssa.name: Technical Standards and Safety Act, 2000, S.O. 2000, c. 16
tssa.use: Administered by the Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA).

reg220_01.name: O. Reg. 220/01 (Boilers and Pressure Vessels)
reg220_01.use: Made under the TSSA Act; adopts CSA B51 (boiler, pressure vessel and pressure piping code).

reg212_01.name: O. Reg. 212/01 (Gaseous Fuels)
reg212_01.use: Made under the TSSA Act; adopts CSA B149.1 (natural gas and propane installation).

reg213_01.name: O. Reg. 213/01 (Fuel Oil)
reg213_01.use: Made under the TSSA Act; adopts CSA B139 (oil-burning equipment).

reg209_01.name: O. Reg. 209/01 (Elevating Devices)
reg209_01.use: Made under the TSSA Act; adopts CSA B44.

reg851.name: R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 851 (Industrial Establishments, under the OHSA)
reg851.use: Applies only to industrial establishments such as factories, plants and warehouses. Hospitals, offices, schools and construction projects fall under other OHSA regulations, so do not raise a pre-start health and safety review (PSR) for them. CSA Z432 (safeguarding of machinery) is the usual design standard for machine guarding.

reg632_05.name: O. Reg. 632/05 (Confined Spaces)
reg632_05.use: Made under the OHSA. Subject to its s. 3 exceptions, it applies to every workplace the Act applies to, including construction projects. Ventilation shafts, plenums, large ducts and fan rooms are confined spaces when they meet its definition.

reg260.name: O. Reg. 260/08 (Performance Standards, under the Professional Engineers Act)
reg260.use: Covers only building construction and demolition, drinking water system evaluations, environmental site assessment reports and tower crane inspections. It does not cover pre-start health and safety reviews; their content is set by `reg851-7`.

obc.name: Ontario Building Code, O. Reg. 163/24
obc.use: Adopts the National Building Code of Canada 2020 with Ontario amendments; it replaced O. Reg. 332/12 on January 1, 2025, which still applies to construction permitted under it. Its mechanical requirements cover heating, ventilating and air-conditioning, plumbing and energy efficiency, but the Part numbers come from the adopted code and have not been confirmed, so do not cite a Part number. Also structural design, fire safety and barrier-free design. Barrier-free design inside buildings, including elevators, is governed by the Building Code.

esc.name: Electrical Safety Code, O. Reg. 164/99
esc.use: Made under the Electricity Act, 1998; covers electrical equipment on machinery and plant, inspected by the Electrical Safety Authority.

epa.name: Environmental Protection Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.19
epa.use: The MECP noise guideline NPC-300 is a guideline, not a regulation.

reg524_98.name: O. Reg. 524/98 (Environmental Compliance Approvals - Exemptions from Section 9 of the Act)
reg524_98.use: Made under the EPA. Equipment it lists does not need an environmental compliance approval under `epa-9`, so check it before saying an approval is needed for ventilation equipment.

reg419_05.name: O. Reg. 419/05 (Air Pollution - Local Air Quality)

reg347.name: R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 347 (General - Waste Management)
reg347.use: Made under the EPA; includes used oils, hydraulic fluid and solvents from removed equipment.

reg463_10.name: O. Reg. 463/10 (Ozone Depleting Substances and Other Halocarbons)
reg463_10.use: Applies only to refrigerants and other halocarbons. For federally owned systems and systems on federal or aboriginal lands, the Federal Halocarbon Regulations apply instead.

eea.name: Energy Efficiency Act, S.C. 1992, c. 36
eea.use: Applies together with the federal Energy Efficiency Regulations.

reg509_18.name: O. Reg. 509/18 (Energy and Water Efficiency - Appliances and Products)

ccpsa.name: Canada Consumer Product Safety Act, S.C. 2010, c. 21

mvsa.name: Motor Vehicle Safety Act, S.C. 1993, c. 16
mvsa.use: For vehicles operated in Ontario, see also the Highway Traffic Act.

hta.name: Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.8

rsa.name: Railway Safety Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 32 (4th Supp.)
rsa.use: Includes the Canadian Rail Operating Rules and train securement rules made under it; rule numbers have not been confirmed.

tdga.name: Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, 1992, S.C. 1992, c. 34
tdga.use: Covers means of containment (for example rail tank cars) and handling of dangerous goods such as crude oil.

clc.name: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2

accord.name: Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Atlantic Accord Implementation and Offshore Renewable Energy Management Act, S.C. 1987, c. 3
accord.use: Formerly the Atlantic Accord Implementation Act.

sor2021_247.name: Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Area Occupational Health and Safety Regulations, SOR/2021-247

sor87_612.name: Oil and Gas Occupational Safety and Health Regulations, SOR/87-612

pea.name: Professional Engineers Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.28

reg941.name: R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 941 (General, under the Professional Engineers Act)
reg941.use: If you need a more specific s. 77 subsection than those listed, cite the whole regulation and say you are not certain of the subsection. A seal means the engineer prepared or actually checked the work: any arrangement where someone seals work they did not prepare, supervise or properly review is an s. 72(2)(e) issue, not only a competence issue.

fppa.name: Fire Protection and Prevention Act, 1997, S.O. 1997, c. 4

firecode.name: Ontario Fire Code, O. Reg. 213/07
firecode.use: Applies to existing buildings, including rapid transit stations, which it defines as a building or part of one used to load and unload passengers of a rapid transit system. Some of its exit door rules do not apply in rapid transit stations that comply with the Building Code.

eaa.name: Environmental Assessment Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.18

owra.name: Ontario Water Resources Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.40

esa.name: Species Conservation Act, 2025, S.O. 2025, c. 4, Sched. 10
esa.use: Replaced the Endangered Species Act, 2007, which was repealed on March 30, 2026.

sara.name: Species at Risk Act, S.C. 2002, c. 29

pps.name: Provincial Planning Statement, 2024 (policy under the Planning Act)
pps.use: Planning decisions must be consistent with it (for example protection of agricultural land, natural heritage and water resources). Cite a section only if you are sure of it.

caa.name: Conservation Authorities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.27

cota.name: City of Toronto Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c. 11, Sched. A
cota.use: Part XVII governs the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC).

tmc591.name: Toronto Municipal Code, Chapter 591 (Noise)
tmc591.use: City of Toronto by-law, checked against the consolidation dated November 14, 2024. The chapter does not say whether construction by or for the TTC counts as government work under `tmc591-3.1`; say it should be confirmed with the City.

aoda.name: Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, S.O. 2005, c. 11

reg191_11.name: O. Reg. 191/11 (Integrated Accessibility Standards)
reg191_11.use: Part IV (transportation standards) applies to public transportation organizations that charge fares, including a municipal transit commission. Do not cite it for building elements such as elevators, ramps, doors or washrooms; cite the Building Code instead.

ohsa.name: Occupational Health and Safety Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.1

ohrc.name: Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19

mfippa.name: Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. M.56
mfippa.use: Privacy: use the law that matches who collects the personal information (municipalities and their local bodies, including a city board or transit commission such as the TTC). It covers only recorded information about an identifiable individual, so ask whether sensors such as passenger counters record images or identifiers.

fippa.name: Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.31
fippa.use: Privacy: use the law that matches who collects the personal information (provincial bodies).

pipeda.name: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, S.C. 2000, c. 5
pipeda.use: Privacy: use the law that matches who collects the personal information (private organizations in commercial activity).

ola.name: Occupiers' Liability Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.2

iaa.name: Impact Assessment Act, S.C. 2019, c. 28, s. 1
iaa.use: Amended in 2024 after the 2023 Supreme Court reference, so flag uncertainty about its current scope.

charter.name: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982)

undrip.name: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, S.C. 2021, c. 14
undrip.use: Free, prior and informed consent is in the Declaration itself, set out in the Act's Schedule, not in the Act's sections.

haida.name: Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73

checks.claim: Safety of pressure equipment, fuels, elevating and amusement devices, administered by TSSA.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1: the purpose is to enhance public safety by administering technical standards for the matters in s. 2. Section 2: the Act applies to amusement devices, boilers and pressure vessels, elevating devices, fuels and operating engineers. The Act's text does not name the Technical Standards and Safety Authority, so who administers it was not confirmed on e-Laws.

checks.claim: Boiler, pressure vessel and piping designs must be registered with TSSA before construction; adopts CSA B51.
checks.sourceSays: Section 4(1): the design of a boiler, pressure vessel, fitting or piping for use in Ontario must be registered with the director; s. 4(2) lets construction start before registration if the person assumes all risks. Codes are adopted through the "Boilers and Pressure Vessels Code Adoption Document" (adopted under O. Reg. 223/01); the regulation itself does not name CSA B51.

checks.claim: Certified operating engineers required for boiler and refrigeration plants above set capacities.
checks.sourceSays: A plant's owner or user designates a chief operating engineer or chief operator for the plant (s. 14). Operating engineers are certified as fourth to first class, and operators as compressor, refrigeration (Class A or B) or steam traction operators (s. 31). The capacity thresholds were not confirmed.

checks.claim: Gaseous fuel appliances and piping; adopts CSA B149.1.
checks.sourceSays: Covers appliances that consume or are intended to consume a gas, with their valves, fittings and controls (s. 1). Codes are adopted through the "Gaseous Fuels Code Adoption Document" (adopted under O. Reg. 223/01); the regulation itself does not name CSA B149.1.

checks.claim: Fuel oil appliances and piping; adopts CSA B139.
checks.sourceSays: Covers fuel oil appliances, tanks and piping (s. 1). Codes are adopted through the "Fuel Oil Code Adoption Document" (adopted under O. Reg. 223/01); the regulation itself does not name CSA B139.

checks.claim: Elevating devices: design registration, inspection and licensing; adopts CSA B44.
checks.sourceSays: Elevating devices need a licence; a "design submission" (drawings, specifications, calculations and test documentation) is submitted to obtain it (s. 1). Codes are adopted through the "Elevating Devices Code Adoption Document" (adopted under O. Reg. 223/01); the regulation itself does not name CSA B44.

checks.claim: Amusement devices: design registration, inspection and licensing.
checks.sourceSays: Section 4(3): no person shall operate an amusement device without a current permit issued by the director; s. 4(4) bars altering it after the permit is issued without the director's consent. The regulation uses permits, not licences; design registration was not confirmed.

checks.claim: A pre-start health and safety review by a professional engineer is required before certain new or modified machinery, apparatus, racking or processes are used in an industrial establishment.
checks.sourceSays: Section 7(2): an owner, lessee or employer must ensure a pre-start health and safety review is conducted when, in a factory, a provision listed in the section's Table applies and a new apparatus, structure, protective element or process is added, or an existing one is modified using new or modified controls. The written report must be signed and dated, and sealed under the Professional Engineers Act if the reviewer is an engineer, so the reviewer is not always an engineer.

checks.claim: Guarding of exposed moving parts of machines.
checks.sourceSays: Section 24: where a machine, prime mover or transmission equipment has an exposed moving part that may endanger a worker, it shall be guarded by a guard or other device that prevents access to the moving part.

checks.claim: Guarding of in-running nip hazards.
checks.sourceSays: Section 25: an in-running nip hazard, or any part of a machine, device or thing that may endanger a worker, shall be guarded by a guard or other device that prevents access to the pinch point.

checks.claim: Work in confined spaces in any workplace, including construction projects.
checks.sourceSays: Section 2: subject to s. 3, the Regulation applies to all workplaces to which the Occupational Health and Safety Act applies. Section 1 defines a confined space as a fully or partially enclosed space that is not both designed and constructed for continuous human occupancy and in which atmospheric hazards may occur because of its construction, location or contents or because of work done in it.

checks.claim: A written confined space program is needed before a worker enters a confined space.
checks.sourceSays: Section 5(1): if a workplace includes a confined space that workers may enter to perform work, the employer shall ensure a written program for it is developed and maintained before a worker enters. Section 5(4): the program must provide for recognizing each confined space, assessing hazards (s. 6), developing plans (s. 7), training workers, and an entry permit system. On a project, s. 5(6) has the employer give a copy to the constructor.

checks.claim: A written hazard assessment of each confined space is needed before any worker enters.
checks.sourceSays: Section 6(1): before any worker enters a confined space, the employer shall ensure an adequate assessment of its hazards has been carried out. Section 6(2): it must be in writing and consider hazards from the space's design, construction, location, use or contents and hazards that may develop during the work. Section 6(5) to (7): it is done by a person with adequate knowledge, training and experience, who signs and dates it.

checks.claim: A separate entry permit is needed each time work is done in a confined space.
checks.sourceSays: Section 10(1): the employer shall ensure a separate entry permit is issued each time work is to be performed in a confined space, before any worker enters. Section 10(2) lists its contents, including the hazards and control measures, the attendant's name, atmospheric test results and provisions for any hot work.

checks.claim: The atmosphere in a confined space must be tested before and during entry.
checks.sourceSays: Section 18(1): the employer shall appoint a person with adequate knowledge, training and experience to perform adequate tests as often as necessary before and while a worker is in a confined space, to ensure acceptable atmospheric levels are maintained. Section 18(3): calibrated instruments appropriate to the hazards must be used; s. 18(4) and (5): results must be recorded.

checks.claim: Performance standards for professional engineers, including the content of a pre-start health and safety review.
checks.sourceSays: O. Reg. 260/08 has four parts: performance standards for building construction, enlargement, alteration and demolition; drinking water system evaluations; environmental site assessment reports; and tower crane inspections. It has no part on pre-start health and safety reviews.

checks.claim: Ontario's building code, including Part 6 (HVAC), Part 7 (plumbing), Part 12 (energy efficiency) and barrier-free design.
checks.sourceSays: The register first cited O. Reg. 332/12, which was revoked on January 1, 2025 (O. Reg. 163/24, s. 3). O. Reg. 163/24, made under the Building Code Act, 1992, adopts the National Building Code of Canada 2020 as amended by the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing's "Ontario Amendments" document as the building code; s. 2 keeps O. Reg. 332/12 for construction permitted by the end of 2024 or designed by then and applied for by March 31, 2025. The Part numbers are in the adopted code, not on e-Laws, and were not checked.

checks.claim: Electrical installations, inspected by the Electrical Safety Authority.
checks.sourceSays: O. Reg. 164/99, made under the Electricity Act, 1998, adopts the Canadian Electrical Code Part 1 (C22.1:24) with the Ontario Amendments issued by the Electrical Safety Authority as the Electrical Safety Code, and applies it to the generation, transmission, distribution, retail and use of electricity in Ontario. Inspection by the Electrical Safety Authority was not confirmed in the text.

checks.claim: An Environmental Compliance Approval is needed for equipment that emits contaminants, including noise and vibration, to the air.
checks.sourceSays: Section 9(1): no person shall, except under an environmental compliance approval, use, operate, construct, alter, extend or replace any plant, structure, equipment, apparatus, mechanism or thing that may discharge a contaminant into any part of the natural environment other than water. Section 1(1) defines "contaminant" to include heat, sound and vibration. Section 9(3) and the regulations set out exceptions.

checks.claim: No discharge of a contaminant that causes or may cause an adverse effect.
checks.sourceSays: Section 14(1): a person shall not discharge a contaminant, or cause or permit its discharge, into the natural environment if the discharge causes or may cause an adverse effect. An amendment not yet in force would change "may cause" to "is likely to cause".

checks.claim: Equipment that brings outdoor air into a building or structure does not need an environmental compliance approval.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1(1), paragraph 6: section 9 of the Act does not apply to any equipment, apparatus, mechanism or thing, other than a cooling tower, that is used for the transfer of outdoor air into a building or structure.

checks.claim: Equipment that exhausts indoor air from a space not used for production, laboratory work or waste handling does not need an environmental compliance approval.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1(1), paragraph 7: section 9 of the Act does not apply to equipment used to ventilate indoor air out of (i) a space used for a purpose other than laboratory analysis, the production, processing, repair, maintenance or storage of goods or materials, or the processing, storage, transfer or disposal of waste, (ii) such a space if the equipment discharges no contaminant from those activities other than heat or noise, (iii) a parking garage, or (iv) a building used solely for handling or baling empty household aerosol cans.

checks.claim: Local air quality standards.
checks.sourceSays: O. Reg. 419/05 (Air Pollution - Local Air Quality), made under the Environmental Protection Act, sets air quality standards for contaminants in Schedule 3 and requires approved dispersion models to show compliance.

checks.claim: Classifying, storing, transporting and disposing of waste, including liquid industrial and hazardous waste.
checks.sourceSays: R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 347 (General - Waste Management), made under the Environmental Protection Act, defines classes of waste, including hazardous waste and liquid industrial waste, and regulates their collection, handling, transportation, storage, processing and disposal.

checks.claim: Refrigerants and other halocarbons must be recovered, not vented; certified technicians required.
checks.sourceSays: Section 19(1): no person shall discharge refrigerant that is or contains a class 2 ozone depleting substance or a halocarbon into the natural environment or within a building. Section 22(1): no person shall service or test refrigeration equipment containing a refrigerant unless certified under s. 34 and with access to equipment that can collect and capture the refrigerant.

checks.claim: Federal Halocarbon Regulations, 2022, SOR/2022-110: apply to federal works and undertakings.
checks.sourceSays: In force (they repealed the 2003 regulations). Section 2(1) applies them to air-conditioning, refrigeration, solvent and fire-extinguishing systems owned by the federal government, a federal board or agency, a Crown corporation or a federal work or undertaking, or located on aboriginal lands or federal lands.

checks.claim: The federal regulations apply to systems owned by the federal government, a Crown corporation or a federal work or undertaking, and to systems on federal or aboriginal lands.
checks.sourceSays: Section 2(1): the Regulations apply to air-conditioning, refrigeration, solvent and fire-extinguishing systems and containers in Canada that are (a) owned by the federal government, a federal board or agency, a Crown corporation or a federal work or undertaking, or (b) located on aboriginal lands or federal lands.

checks.claim: Energy Efficiency Act, S.C. 1992, c. 36: minimum efficiency for regulated energy-using products.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Energy Efficiency Act as S.C. 1992, c. 36; its long title covers the energy efficiency of energy-using products.

checks.claim: Ontario minimum efficiency standards for appliances and products.
checks.sourceSays: e-Laws lists O. Reg. 509/18 (Energy and Water Efficiency - Appliances and Products), made under the Electricity Act, 1998. Its requirements for particular appliances and products refer in places to the federal Energy Efficiency Regulations, 2016.

checks.claim: Canada Consumer Product Safety Act, S.C. 2010, c. 21: consumer products must not pose an unreasonable danger to health or safety.
checks.sourceSays: S.C. 2010, c. 21. The Act defines "danger to human health or safety" as any unreasonable hazard posed by a consumer product during normal or foreseeable use.

checks.claim: Manufacturers and importers must not sell a consumer product that is a danger to human health or safety.
checks.sourceSays: Section 7: no manufacturer or importer shall manufacture, import, advertise or sell a consumer product that (a) is a danger to human health or safety, or (b) is the subject of a recall order.

checks.claim: Manufacturers and importers must not sell a consumer product that is a danger to human health or safety.
checks.sourceSays: Section 7(a): no manufacturer or importer shall manufacture, import, advertise or sell a consumer product that is a danger to human health or safety.

checks.claim: Motor Vehicle Safety Act, S.C. 1993, c. 16: federal safety standards for new vehicles and vehicle equipment.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Motor Vehicle Safety Act as S.C. 1993, c. 16.

checks.claim: Rules for vehicles operated in Ontario.
checks.sourceSays: e-Laws lists the Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.8, in force.

checks.claim: Railway Safety Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 32 (4th Supp.): safety of federally regulated railways, including operating rules made under it.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Railway Safety Act as R.S.C. 1985, c. 32 (4th Supp.). Rule numbers in the Canadian Rail Operating Rules were not checked.

checks.claim: The Act applies only to railways within the legislative authority of Parliament.
checks.sourceSays: Section 2(2): this Act applies in respect of railways that are within the legislative authority of Parliament. Section 4(1) defines "railway" as a railway within the legislative authority of Parliament, including its tunnels and stations.

checks.claim: Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, 1992, S.C. 1992, c. 34: means of containment and handling of dangerous goods.
checks.sourceSays: S.C. 1992, c. 34. The Act defines "means of containment" as a container or packaging, or any part of a means of transport that is or can be used to contain goods.

checks.claim: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2, Part II: occupational health and safety for federally regulated workplaces.
checks.sourceSays: R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2. Part II is titled "Occupational Health and Safety" and begins at s. 122.

checks.claim: Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Atlantic Accord Implementation Act, S.C. 1987, c. 3: offshore oil and gas safety off Newfoundland and Labrador.
checks.sourceSays: Short title: Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Atlantic Accord Implementation and Offshore Renewable Energy Management Act, S.C. 1987, c. 3 (renamed by S.C. 2024, c. 20, s. 2; formerly the Atlantic Accord Implementation Act). Part III.1 (s. 205.001 onward) covers occupational health and safety in the offshore area.

checks.claim: Offshore occupational health and safety off Newfoundland and Labrador.
checks.sourceSays: Part III.1 of the Act is titled "Occupational Health and Safety" (s. 205.001 onward).

checks.claim: Occupational health and safety rules for the Newfoundland and Labrador offshore area.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Canada–Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Area Occupational Health and Safety Regulations as SOR/2021-247, made under the Atlantic Accord Act.

checks.claim: Oil and Gas Occupational Safety and Health Regulations, SOR/87-612: offshore safety off Newfoundland and Labrador, including standby vessels.
checks.sourceSays: In force, made under the Canada Labour Code. Section 1.3 applies it to oil and gas work in "Canada lands" as defined in the Canada Oil and Gas Act; the Newfoundland and Labrador offshore area is covered instead by Part III.1 of the Atlantic Accord Act and SOR/2021-247. Section 18.15 requires a standby craft able to evacuate all employees from drilling and production operations.

checks.claim: A standby craft able to evacuate all employees is required for drilling and production operations.
checks.sourceSays: Section 18.15: for every drilling operation and production operation, the employer shall provide a standby craft capable of safely evacuating all employees from the work place.

checks.claim: The regulations apply to oil and gas work on Canada lands.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1.3(1): the Regulations (other than Part II) apply to employees in exploration, drilling, production, conservation, processing or transportation of oil or gas in Canada lands as defined in the Canada Oil and Gas Act; s. 1.3(3) excludes employees operating ships or aircraft.

checks.claim: Ontario statute governing the practice of professional engineering.
checks.sourceSays: e-Laws lists the Professional Engineers Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.28, in force. It sets up the Association and governs licensing and the practice of professional engineering (for example s. 12).

checks.claim: A licence is required to practise professional engineering or to hold oneself out as doing so.
checks.sourceSays: Section 12(1): no person shall engage in the practice of professional engineering, or hold themselves out as doing so, unless they hold a licence, temporary licence, provisional licence or limited licence. Section 12(2) also requires a certificate of authorization to offer engineering services to the public; s. 12(3) to (6) set out exceptions.

checks.claim: Offences for practising or using the title without a licence.
checks.sourceSays: Section 40(1): contravening s. 12 is an offence (fine of up to $25,000 for a first offence and $50,000 after). Section 40(2): a person without a licence or temporary licence who uses the title "professional engineer", uses "engineer" in a way that suggests they may practise, or uses a seal suggesting they are a professional engineer commits an offence (up to $10,000, then $25,000).

checks.claim: General regulation under the Professional Engineers Act; often cited as "O. Reg. 941".
checks.sourceSays: e-Laws lists it as R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 941 (General), made under the Professional Engineers Act. "O. Reg. 941" is an informal name, not its official citation.

checks.claim: Code of Ethics: duty to act with fairness and loyalty, fidelity to public needs, personal honour and professional integrity, knowledge and competence.
checks.sourceSays: There is no s. 77.1; this is s. 77, paragraph 1 of the Code of Ethics. It is the duty of a practitioner to the public, their employer, clients, other members of the profession and themselves to act at all times with (i) fairness and loyalty to associates, employer, clients, subordinates and employees, (ii) fidelity to public needs, (iii) devotion to high ideals of personal honour and professional integrity, (iv) knowledge of developments relevant to the services undertaken, and (v) competence in performing them.

checks.claim: The practitioner shall regard the duty for public welfare as paramount.
checks.sourceSays: Section 77, paragraph 2, subparagraph i: a practitioner shall regard the practitioner's duty to public welfare as paramount. e-Laws numbers it as part of s. 77, not as s. 77.2(i).

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: negligence.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(a): professional misconduct means negligence. Section 72(1) defines negligence as an act or omission in the practitioner's work that fails to maintain the standards a reasonable and prudent practitioner would maintain in the circumstances.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: failure to make reasonable provision for safeguarding life, health or property.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(b): failure to make reasonable provision for the safeguarding of life, health or property of a person who may be affected by the work for which the practitioner is responsible.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: failure to act to correct or report a situation that may endanger safety or welfare of the public.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(c): failure to act to correct or report a situation that the practitioner believes may endanger the safety or the welfare of the public.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: failure to make responsible provision for complying with applicable statutes, regulations, standards, codes and by-laws.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(d): failure to make responsible provision for complying with applicable statutes, regulations, standards, codes, by-laws and rules in connection with work being undertaken by or under the responsibility of the practitioner.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: signing or sealing a document not actually prepared or checked by the practitioner.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(e): signing, dating or sealing an engineering document, or failing to do one or more of them, in contravention of section 53. Section 53(2) requires a practitioner to sign, date and seal an engineering document whose engineering content they prepared or for which they otherwise assume responsibility.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: failure to present clearly to the employer the consequences of overruling the practitioner's engineering judgment.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(f): failure to present clearly to the employer the consequences to be expected from a deviation proposed in work, if the practitioner's professional engineering judgment is overruled by non-technical authority where the practitioner is responsible for the technical adequacy of the work.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: undertaking work the practitioner is not competent to perform.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(h): undertaking work the practitioner is not competent to perform by virtue of the practitioner's training and experience.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: failure to disclose a conflict of interest.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(i): failure to make prompt, voluntary and complete disclosure of an interest, direct or indirect, that might be construed as prejudicial to the practitioner's professional judgment in serving the public, an employer or a client, with listed examples such as accepting compensation from more than one party.

checks.claim: Professional misconduct: conduct regarded as disgraceful, dishonourable or unprofessional.
checks.sourceSays: Section 72(2)(j): conduct or an act relevant to the practice of professional engineering that, having regard to all the circumstances, would reasonably be regarded by the engineering profession as disgraceful, dishonourable or unprofessional.

checks.claim: Statute under which the Building Code is made; building permits.
checks.sourceSays: Section 8(1): no person shall construct or demolish a building, or cause one to be constructed or demolished, unless the chief building official has issued a permit. The building code, O. Reg. 163/24, is made under this Act.

checks.claim: Fire protection and prevention in Ontario; the Fire Code is made under it.
checks.sourceSays: S.O. 1997, c. 4. Section 1(1) defines "fire code" as the fire code established under Part IV of the Act; the Fire Code, O. Reg. 213/07, is made under it.

checks.claim: Fire safety of existing buildings and facilities.
checks.sourceSays: O. Reg. 213/07 (Fire Code), made under the Fire Protection and Prevention Act, 1997. Article 2.1.1.2: Part 2 applies to buildings, premises, tents, air-supported structures and outdoor public amusement areas.

checks.claim: Disconnect switches for air-conditioning and ventilating systems must be tested at least every 12 months to show the system can be shut down in an emergency.
checks.sourceSays: Article 2.6.1.8(1): disconnect switches for mechanical air-conditioning and ventilating systems shall be tested at intervals not greater than 12 months to establish that the system can be shut down in an emergency. Sentence (2) exempts systems serving only a single residential suite. Article 2.6.1.7: heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems shall be operated and maintained so as not to create a hazardous condition.

checks.claim: Hot work on ducts is allowed only once the system is shut down and the duct is cleaned of combustible deposits.
checks.sourceSays: Article 2.6.1.10(1): no work on ducts involving hot work equipment shall be performed unless (a) the system has been shut down, (b) the duct has been cleaned of any accumulations of combustible deposits, and (c) any combustible lining and covering material that could be ignited by the work has been removed.

checks.claim: The fire safety plan must cover shutdowns of fire protection systems and must be revised before construction starts.
checks.sourceSays: Article 2.8.2.1: a fire safety plan shall be prepared, approved and implemented in buildings to which Section 2.8 applies. It must include documents showing the type, location and operation of the building's fire emergency systems ((2)(d)) and provide alternative measures for occupant safety during a shutdown of any fire protection equipment or systems ((2)(h)). Before demolition or construction starts, it must be revised to add temporary alternative fire safety measures and temporary procedures to control the work's fire hazards ((5)), and the revised plan must be implemented ((6)). Article 2.8.1.1 lists the buildings Section 2.8 applies to, including those containing an assembly occupancy or with 4 or more storeys counting storeys below grade; which occupancy a subway station is was not confirmed.

checks.claim: Environmental assessment of provincial public-sector and designated projects.
checks.sourceSays: Section 2: the purpose is the protection, conservation and wise management of Ontario's environment. The Act applies to "undertakings", defined to include activities by or on behalf of the Crown, a public body or a municipality, and major commercial activities designated by regulation, and to "designated projects" (Part II.3 and Part II.4 projects). Part II.1 covers class environmental assessments.

checks.claim: Protection of Ontario's surface and ground water.
checks.sourceSays: Section 0.1: the purpose is to provide for the conservation, protection and management of Ontario's waters and their efficient and sustainable use. Section 1(1) defines "water" as surface water and ground water.

checks.claim: Protection of species at risk and their habitat in Ontario.
checks.sourceSays: The register first cited the Endangered Species Act, 2007, which was repealed on March 30, 2026 (S.O. 2025, c. 4, Sched. 10, s. 68) and replaced by the Species Conservation Act, 2025, S.O. 2025, c. 4, Sched. 10. Its s. 1 purposes are to identify species at risk using the best available scientific information, including community knowledge and Indigenous traditional knowledge, and to protect and conserve species at risk while taking into account social and economic considerations, including sustainable economic growth.

checks.claim: Species at Risk Act, S.C. 2002, c. 29.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Species at Risk Act as S.C. 2002, c. 29.

checks.claim: Land use planning and municipal approvals.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1.1: the purposes include a land use planning system led by provincial policy, integrating provincial interests in provincial and municipal planning decisions, fair and open planning processes, and recognizing the decision-making authority and accountability of municipal councils in planning.

checks.claim: Provincial policy that land use planning decisions must be consistent with.
checks.sourceSays: Ontario.ca: the Provincial Planning Statement, 2024 is issued under section 3 of the Planning Act, which requires all decisions affecting planning matters to be consistent with it. It replaced the Provincial Policy Statement, 2020 and the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe, 2019.

checks.claim: Permits for development in or near watercourses, wetlands, valleys and shorelines.
checks.sourceSays: Section 28(1): in a conservation authority's area, no person shall straighten, change, divert or interfere with a watercourse or wetland, or carry out development in hazardous lands, wetlands, river or stream valleys, or shoreline areas that may be affected by flooding, erosion or dynamic beach hazards. Section 28 sets the prohibitions; the permits that allow these activities were not checked.

checks.claim: The Toronto Transit Commission is continued as a city board.
checks.sourceSays: Section 394(1): the Toronto Transit Commission is continued as a city board. Section 394(2): the TTC is deemed to be a street railway company for the purposes of The Railways Act, R.S.O. 1950, c. 331.

checks.claim: Only the TTC may establish, operate or maintain a local passenger transportation system in Toronto.
checks.sourceSays: Section 395(1): no person other than the TTC shall establish, operate or maintain a local passenger transportation system within the City until the TTC is dissolved or control of the system is removed from it. Section 395(3) lists exceptions, including railway companies incorporated under federal or provincial statutes and taxicabs; s. 395(5) lets the TTC agree to let another municipality or local board operate part of its system in the City.

checks.claim: Construction noise that is clearly audible is prohibited from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. (9 a.m. on Saturdays) and all day on Sundays and statutory holidays.
checks.sourceSays: § 591-2.3: no person shall emit or cause or permit sound from construction or construction equipment that is clearly audible (A) from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. the next day, except until 9 a.m. on Saturdays, and/or (B) all day on Sundays and statutory holidays. § 591-1.1 defines construction to include alteration, repair, equipment installation and alteration.

checks.claim: Sound limits for stationary sources, such as fixed fans, measured at a point of reception in a living area.
checks.sourceSays: § 591-2.8(A): no person shall cause or permit sound from a stationary source exceeding, as a one-hour Leq at an outdoor point of reception in a living area, 45 dB(A) from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. or 50 dB(A) from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m., or the limit in provincial noise guidelines if applicable; (B) indoor limits are 40 and 45 dB(A). (C) These limits do not apply to a stationary source that complies with a provincial environmental compliance approval or is registered on the Environmental Activity and Sector Registry. § 591-1.1 defines a living area as the premises of a dwelling or a workplace.

checks.claim: Government work is exempt from the noise prohibitions.
checks.sourceSays: § 591-3.1: despite any other provision, it is lawful to emit sound from, among other things, (A) bells or whistles operated by rail or transit services for public safety, (B) emergency measures, and (D) government work. § 591-1.1 defines government work as construction, rehabilitation or maintenance work conducted by the City, the Province of Ontario, the Government of Canada and any of its agencies or agents, including vehicles and equipment actually engaged in the work.

checks.claim: A noise exemption permit can be applied for at least 28 days before the activity.
checks.sourceSays: § 591-3.2(A): any person may apply for an exemption permit from a noise prohibition by filing with the Executive Director at least 28 calendar days before the activity, with any information requested, including a noise mitigation plan and a statement certified by a professional engineer or acoustical consultant for sounds that cannot feasibly be controlled. (B.1, C) Ward councillors are notified before a permit is issued. (G) The City and its agencies, boards and commissions apply directly and pay no fees.

checks.claim: Accessibility standards for Ontario.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1: the purpose is to benefit all Ontarians by developing, implementing and enforcing accessibility standards for goods, services, facilities, accommodation, employment, buildings, structures and premises, with the involvement of persons with disabilities.

checks.claim: Design of Public Spaces: mainly outdoor spaces, paths, parking and service areas.
checks.sourceSays: Part IV.1, Design of Public Spaces Standards (Accessibility Standards for the Built Environment), covers recreational trails and beach access routes, outdoor public use eating areas, outdoor play spaces, exterior paths of travel, accessible parking, obtaining services, and maintenance of accessible elements.

checks.claim: Transportation Standards: accessibility duties of public transit providers, including subways.
checks.sourceSays: Part IV, Transportation Standards (ss. 33 to 80). Section 33 defines a conventional transportation service provider as a designated public sector transportation organization described in paragraph 5 of Schedule 1 that provides conventional transportation services, which include rail-based transportation, operating solely within Ontario. Schedule 1, paragraph 5 covers every public transportation organization in Ontario that charges a fare and whose vehicles are operated by, for or on behalf of the Government of Ontario, a municipality, a local board of a municipality or a transit or transportation commission or authority.

checks.claim: Transit providers must have public emergency preparedness and response policies for the safety of persons with disabilities.
checks.sourceSays: Section 37(1): conventional and specialized transportation service providers shall establish, implement, maintain and document emergency preparedness and response policies that provide for the safety of persons with disabilities, and make them available to the public. Section 37(2): on request, they must be provided in an accessible format.

checks.claim: When subway service is temporarily changed and the change is known in advance, the provider must offer accessible alternate arrangements and communicate them accessibly.
checks.sourceSays: Section 50(1): where a route or scheduled service is temporarily changed and the change is known before the trip begins, conventional transportation service providers shall (a) make available alternate accessible arrangements to transfer persons with disabilities to their route destination where the alternate arrangements for persons without disabilities are inaccessible, and (b) communicate information on the alternate arrangements in a manner that takes the person's disability into account. Section 50(2) applies this to subways, among other modes.

checks.claim: A provider must give public notice of a temporary disruption in facilities or services that persons with disabilities usually use, with the reason, expected duration and alternatives.
checks.sourceSays: Section 80.48(1): if persons with disabilities usually use particular facilities or services of a provider and there is a temporary disruption in them, the provider shall give notice of the disruption to the public. Section 80.48(2): the notice must include the reason, the anticipated duration and a description of any alternative facilities or services. Section 80.48(3): every provider other than a small organization must prepare a document setting out the steps it will take for a temporary disruption. Section 80.48(5): notice may be posted at a conspicuous place on the premises or on the provider's website.

checks.claim: Workplace health and safety in Ontario.
checks.sourceSays: e-Laws lists the Occupational Health and Safety Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.1, in force. Regulations made under it include O. Reg. 213/91 (Construction Projects) and R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 851 (Industrial Establishments).

checks.claim: Health and safety on construction projects.
checks.sourceSays: O. Reg. 213/91 (Construction Projects), made under the Occupational Health and Safety Act. Section 20: Part II (General Construction) applies to all projects.

checks.claim: Equal treatment and freedom from discrimination, including in services and facilities.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1: every person has a right to equal treatment with respect to services, goods and facilities, without discrimination because of race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability.

checks.claim: Privacy of personal information collected by municipalities.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1(b): a purpose of the Act is to protect the privacy of individuals with respect to personal information held by institutions. "Institution" is defined to include a municipality and local bodies such as a transit commission, school board or police service board.

checks.claim: An institution may collect personal information only when a statute expressly authorizes it, for law enforcement, or when it is necessary to the proper administration of a lawfully authorized activity.
checks.sourceSays: Section 28(2): no person shall collect personal information on behalf of an institution unless the collection is expressly authorized by statute, used for the purposes of law enforcement or necessary to the proper administration of a lawfully authorized activity.

checks.claim: From January 1, 2027, an institution must prepare a written privacy impact assessment before collecting personal information.
checks.sourceSays: Section 28(3), added by S.O. 2026, c. 2, Sched. 11, s. 9(2) and in force January 1, 2027: unless the regulations provide otherwise, before collecting personal information the head of an institution shall ensure a written assessment is prepared covering, among other things, the purpose and why the information is necessary, the legal authority, the types and sources of information, who will have access, the retention period, safeguards and risks, and steps to prevent and mitigate theft, loss or unauthorized use. Section 28(4): those steps must be implemented before collection, or within a reasonable time after if that is not possible. Section 28(5): the assessment must be updated before any significant change of purpose.

checks.claim: People must be told the legal authority and purpose for collecting their personal information, and who can answer questions about it.
checks.sourceSays: Section 29(2): if personal information is collected on behalf of an institution, the head shall inform the individual of (a) the legal authority for the collection, (b) the principal purposes for which it will be used, and (c) the title, business address and business telephone number of an officer or employee who can answer questions about it. Section 29(3) sets out exceptions, including law enforcement.

checks.claim: Privacy of personal information collected by provincial bodies.
checks.sourceSays: Section 1(b): a purpose of the Act is to protect the privacy of individuals with respect to personal information held by institutions, and to give them a right of access to it.

checks.claim: PIPEDA, S.C. 2000, c. 5: privacy for private organizations in commercial activity.
checks.sourceSays: S.C. 2000, c. 5. Section 4(1)(a): Part 1 applies to personal information an organization collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities.

checks.claim: Part 1 applies to organizations handling personal information in commercial activities.
checks.sourceSays: Section 4(1): Part 1 applies to personal information that (a) the organization collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities, or (b) is about an employee of, or applicant to, a federal work, undertaking or business.

checks.claim: PIPEDA applies to personal information collected, used or disclosed in commercial activities.
checks.sourceSays: Section 4(1)(a): Part 1 applies to personal information that the organization collects, uses or discloses in the course of commercial activities.

checks.claim: Duty of occupiers to keep people on their premises reasonably safe.
checks.sourceSays: Section 3(1): an occupier owes a duty to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that persons entering the premises, and their property, are reasonably safe while on the premises.

checks.claim: Impact Assessment Act, S.C. 2019, c. 28, s. 1: federal assessment of designated projects; amended in 2024.
checks.sourceSays: Justice Laws lists the Act as S.C. 2019, c. 28, s. 1 (it was enacted by section 1 of that chapter), with amendments by S.C. 2024, c. 17.

checks.claim: Parliament has authority over classes of subjects expressly excepted from the provinces' powers.
checks.sourceSays: Section 91, class 29: "Such Classes of Subjects as are expressly excepted in the Enumeration of the Classes of Subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the Provinces."

checks.claim: Railways and other works connecting provinces or extending beyond a province are excepted from provincial power.
checks.sourceSays: Section 92(10)(a) excepts from provincial "Local Works and Undertakings" lines of ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works connecting the province with others or extending beyond its limits.

checks.claim: Federal legislative powers.
checks.sourceSays: Section 91 sets out the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada.

checks.claim: Provincial legislative powers.
checks.sourceSays: Section 92 sets out the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures.

checks.claim: Aboriginal and treaty rights are recognized and affirmed.
checks.sourceSays: Section 35(1): "The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed."

checks.claim: Existing Aboriginal and treaty rights are recognized and affirmed.
checks.sourceSays: Section 35(1): "The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed."

checks.claim: Equality before and under the law without discrimination.
checks.sourceSays: Section 15(1): every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination.

checks.claim: Equality rights.
checks.sourceSays: Section 15(1): every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination.

checks.claim: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, S.C. 2021, c. 14 (free, prior and informed consent).
checks.sourceSays: S.C. 2021, c. 14. Free, prior and informed consent appears in the Declaration itself, which is reproduced in the Act's Schedule (for example Articles 10 and 11), not in the Act's own sections.

checks.claim: Haida Nation v. British Columbia, 2004 SCC 73: the Crown's duty to consult; procedural parts may be delegated to proponents.
checks.sourceSays: 2004 SCC 73, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 511. Para. 53: the Crown alone remains legally responsible for consultation and accommodation, but it may delegate procedural aspects of consultation to industry proponents seeking a particular development; the honour of the Crown cannot be delegated.
